reader.title: Marion election riot and arrest of Martin Malone
bases: An election-day riot at the Marion polls in which Black men were said to have shot and killed white men, followed by a sheriff's posse siege of a white Republican's house, a pursuit in which fleeing Black men were fired on, and arrests including Martin Malone's on Nov. 9 (A1, A2, A8, A16); Malone himself was jailed unharmed, and whether the posse killed Black men is disputed (A3, A16).

Martin Malone was arrested by a sheriff's search party of fifty (or fifteen) and jailed, with no harm reported (A2, A4); the wider posse acted with warrants under Sheriff Henderson, and the report that it shot and killed fleeing Black men comes from one Republican letter and is denied by the Democratic dispatch (A16, A3).

The riot and the siege are reported in several independent dispatches and letters (A1, A2, A8, A9), but Malone's arrest rests on a single Meridian dispatch (A2, A3), and Republican letters contradict the Democratic account of who began the shooting and whether Black men were killed (A14, A16, A17).

summary.text: The Marion election riot was a shooting at the polls in Marion, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, on November 8, 1881, followed by a sheriff's posse siege of a white Republican's house, a pursuit of fleeing Black men, and the arrest of a Black man, Martin Malone, on November 9.
Several white men died at the polls, and at the house the posse killed John Vance and lost A. G. Warren.
Democratic reports blamed Black voters and the Vances; Republican correspondents said the posse shot down Black men.

Marion Station lay five or six miles from Meridian, and a Republican correspondent called it the county's only Republican precinct, with 'trouble' at every election; Ed Vance, described as the county's Republican leader, lived two miles away.
According to a Meridian dispatch of November 10, a Black man insulted Joseph Barnett at the polls, and when Barnett raised his arm, Frank Johnson shot him dead.
Jeff Segars and Alexander Harvey, the Democratic candidate for assessor, were then killed, and George Johnson, a Black man once Barnett's slave, was shot and died two days later.
The dispatch named the shooters as Gillespie, Frank Johnson, Allen and Burwell Brown, and Martin Malone, and said Will Vance gave the word to fire.
Sheriff R. L. Henderson came from Meridian with seventy-five men, and an advance party carrying warrants was fired on and driven back from Ed Vance's house.
About five o'clock a white flag was shown and a surrender agreed, but John Vance was shot dead by the posse and Warren was killed by a shot from the house.
Ed Vance escaped with thirty or forty Black men, and 'many shots were fired at them as they retreated,' as the Jackson Clarion put it.
E. H. Dial's election-night letter said several were shot by the posse as they ran through the bushes.
On November 9 a party under the sheriff's direction, fifty men in most copies and fifteen in the New-York Tribune, searched for those concerned in the riot.
It found only Martin Malone, 'who took an active part in the riot,' and he was lodged in jail, with no harm to him reported.
Four more Black men, among them Jacob Johnson, Green Johnson and Jacob Nailer, were jailed about November 19, and seven were in the Meridian jail by December 10.
A New York Times correspondent wrote on December 1 that Will Vance had been held nearly a month without a charge.
William Vance's preliminary examination as an accessory to the murders opened in Meridian on December 22.
An anonymous letter at Meridian warned Black route agents to resign their posts because of 'the late trouble caused by your race at Marlon.'
No report of an examination, indictment or trial of Martin Malone appears in the coverage.

The November 10 dispatch ran nationally the next day under headlines such as 'Murder at the Polls' (Savannah) and 'Several White Men Killed by Colored Men' (New York), and reached Mississippi weeklies a week later.
The Chicago Tribune labeled it 'A Democratic Account' and put 'Election' in quotation marks.
Mississippi papers called it 'The Massacre at Marion' and 'The Marion Horror,' and the Greenville Times spoke of a 'negro outrage.'
Republican letters answered in December under headlines such as 'Victims of Bourbon Hate' and 'The Bottom Facts of the Mississippi Massacre.'
The same report of Will Vance's examination appeared in Memphis as the trial of the 'Principal Instigator' of a 'Bloody Election Massacre' and in Washington as 'The Farce of Trying Republicans.'
Malone appeared only in the November 10 dispatch, as a name on the list of shooters and as the one man the search party caught.
The dispatch said a Black man fired before Barnett could strike; the National Republican's correspondent said Barnett clubbed Gillespie and a Segars fired first.
At Will Vance's examination, the Black witness Julius Jackson testified that Barnett tore up Gillespie's ticket and struck him, and that Harvey had a pistol.

The dispatch said 'none were murdered in the swamps,' but the Greenville Times reported the opinion that all the fleeing men had been slain, and the National Republican said a number were shot and killed.

accounts.label: Meridian Nov. 10 dispatch (Democratic account)
accounts.gist: A negro insulted Barnett, Frank Johnson shot him, and Black men from another precinct killed unarmed whites at Will Vance's word; at Vance's house John Vance levelled a gun and was shot, Warren was killed from the house, no negroes were known killed, and Malone alone was found by the Nov. 9 search and jailed.

accounts.label: Dial letter to the Democratic state chairman
accounts.gist: An 'impudent' negro insulted an old man, negroes fired, and about a hundred negroes fortified Vance's house; Warren was shot at the well under a flag of truce, and several fleeing negroes were shot by the posse in the bushes.

accounts.label: New York Herald account (Greenville Times)
accounts.gist: A negro refused a vote as a non-resident returned with armed men; 200 armed negroes gathered at Vance's; the fleeing negroes were pursued by armed men from Kemper County and Meridian and were thought to have all been slain.

accounts.label: Republican correspondents (New York Times; National Republican)
accounts.gist: Barnett struck Gillespie and a Segars fired first; John Vance was shot dead by the posse without cause and a number of fleeing Black men were killed; Will Vance was held without a charge and Ed Vance had nothing to do with the riot.

accounts.label: Testimony at Will Vance's examination
accounts.gist: Prosecution witnesses said the Vances prompted the shooting and negroes held 75 to 100 pistols; Julius Jackson (colored) said Barnett tore up Gillespie's ticket and struck him, and that some whites, Harvey among them, had pistols.

framing.detail: Mississippi Democratic papers headed it 'The Massacre at Marion' and 'The Marion Horror', stressed that the whites were unarmed, and spoke of a 'negro outrage'.

Northern and Southern dailies ran the Nov. 10 Meridian dispatch as 'Murder at the Polls' or 'Several White Men Killed by Colored Men'; the Chicago Tribune labeled it 'A Democratic Account' and put 'Election' in quotation marks.
Republican letters headed 'Victims of Bourbon Hate' and 'The Bottom Facts of the Mississippi Massacre' said colored men were shot down and the facts distorted by wire.
The Dec. 22 examination report ran under opposite headlines: 'Principal Instigator ... Bloody Election Massacre' in Memphis and 'The Farce of Trying Republicans' in Washington.

versions.value: A negro insulted Barnett and Frank Johnson shot him before he could strike; the whites were unarmed.
Barnett struck Gillespie with a club, and the fight began with a Segars firing the first shot.
Barnett tore up Gillespie's ticket, Gillespie kicked him, Barnett struck him with a stick; some whites had pistols.

conflicts.note: The Dec. 22 testimony was given under examination and includes a Black witness; the Nov. 10 dispatch was compiled from 'participants' and labeled Democratic by the Chicago Tribune.

versions.value: No negroes known killed; four or five wounded; none murdered in the swamps.
Several fleeing negroes shot by the posse.
Prevailing opinion that all the fleeing negroes were slain in the woods.
A number of the colored men fleeing Vance's house were shot and killed.

conflicts.note: No account names a Black man killed by the posse.

conflicts.field: size of the Nov. 9 search party
conflicts.note: Same dispatch; likely a transmission variant.

conflicts.field: death of John Vance and Warren

versions.value: John Vance levelled a gun at the posse and was shot; Warren was shot from the house while pledging protection or drinking at the well.
John Vance rode up unarmed in the fight and was shot dead by the posse; Warren, threatening Mrs. Vance, was then shot by a Vance brother, inside the front gate.

conflicts.note: Each version comes from a partisan correspondent.

record_check.dossier: Nov. 9 is the date of Malone's arrest; the riot and siege were on election day, Nov. 8.
Marion (Marion Station), with the siege at Ed Vance's house about two miles away.

record_check.record: Martin Malone, Ed Vance, John Vance, Will Vance, Jeff Segars, Alex Harvey, Harden Jones, Joseph Barnett, George Johnson, A. G. Warren
record_check.dossier: Mixes the arrested Black man (Malone), the white Vances, the white dead at the polls, a posse member (Warren) and a wounded posse member (Jones); the Black targets of posse violence were Malone and the unnamed men fired on while fleeing.
Sheriff R. L. Henderson's posse and a search party under his direction.
Disputed: none by the posse per the dispatch, 'a number' per the National Republican; George Johnson (colored) was killed at the polls by a negro per the dispatch.
Four at the polls in early reports plus John Vance and A. G. Warren.

Six or seven reported (four whites at the polls, George Johnson, John Vance, Warren), with Vince Segars dead in early reports but 'expected to die' in later ones, plus any Black men killed in the pursuit.
Malone himself was arrested and jailed; the killing and shooting belong to the riot, the siege and the pursuit.

info: Riot at the polls on election day, Tuesday Nov. 8, 1881; the search party that arrested Martin Malone went out on Nov. 9 ('yesterday' in a Nov. 10 dispatch).
Marion (Marion Station), five to six miles from Meridian; the siege took place at Ed Vance's house about two miles from Marion.

Martin Malone (a 'negro') arrested and jailed; Black men fleeing Vance's house fired on (wounded or, in one account, killed); white dead at the polls Joseph Barnett/Barret/Burnett, Jeff Segars, Alexander Harvey, and Vince Segars (dead in early reports, 'expected to die' later); George Johnson (colored) shot at the polls and died Nov. 10; at Vance's house John Vance (white) and A. G. Warren of the posse killed.
Malone was named among the negroes said to have done the shooting at the polls and was said to have 'taken an active part in the riot.'
Sheriff R. L. Henderson's posse from Meridian; the search party of Nov. 9 went 'under direction of the Sheriff.'

Disputed: the Nov. 10 dispatch says no negroes known killed and four or five wounded (George Johnson, colored, shot at the polls by a negro, died Nov. 10); the National Republican letter says a number of the Black men fleeing Vance's house were shot and killed.

sources.note: Meridian Nov. 8 dispatch: four whites killed at Marion Station, siege of Ed Vance's house, John Vance and A. G. Warren killed, 30 or 40 negroes fled to the woods under fire; no Malone.
